RegisterIn.description:
What a stranger may state about themself: who they are and a password. Nothing else.

`caps` and `roles` USED TO BE FIELDS HERE, and this route is unauthenticated. Anyone able to
reach it could send caps=["*"] and receive a token that satisfies every capability check on
the platform — the gateway honours "*" as a wildcard — for any tenant they named. That is a
total compromise reachable by one POST, and REGISTRATION_ENABLED defaults to true.

They are not validated here; they are ABSENT. Pydantic ignores unknown fields, so an existing
client that still sends them keeps working and the values are discarded — a 400 would only
tell an attacker which field to rename. Privilege comes from the server, never the request.

core/tenancy.py already said this for the multi-tenant path: "a request may ASK for a tenant;
it may never SUPPLY one", and "caps and roles come from the Membership". This legacy
single-tenant route bypassed that guard entirely.
RegisterIn.title: RegisterIn

post.description:
Ask for another verification mail. ALWAYS 202, whatever the truth.

This route is unauthenticated, so every distinguishable outcome is an oracle: whether the
address is registered, whether it is already verified, whether it is in cooldown. All of them
answer the same way. A caller who owns the address learns the truth from their inbox, which is
the only place that should be telling them.

Choose ONE door and get a token scoped to it.

This is THE mint, and it is the only door between every company on the platform. The tenant
that ends up in the token is read off the membership row we find — never off `body.tenant`
(T1). `body.tenant` is a request to be let in, not an assertion of where you already are.

Redeem a verification token. Single-use.

Unknown, expired and already-spent are ONE answer on purpose. Distinguishing them tells an
attacker holding a stale link whether the address exists and whether someone got there first,
and none of those distinctions helps a legitimate user — who needs the same next step in
every case: ask for another mail.

Who works HERE. Admin-gated, one tenant, paginated.

THE TENANT IS NOT A PARAMETER. It is read off the caller's token — the same membership row the
mint verified. A `?tenant=` on a directory read is T1 wearing a different hat: it would let any
admin enumerate the staff of any company on the platform, and it would look like a feature.

A caller with no tenant claim is REJECTED, never widened to "all tenants" (T8).

Change a member's roles/caps in THIS tenant — never their credential (T2).

Without this, changing what a member may do meant removing and re-inviting them: it dropped the
membership and forced a fresh password claim. This edits only the roles/caps on the membership.
A role change is a change in who holds power, so it is audited write-ahead as critical.

get.description:
Answer a question another service declared identity as the OWNER of.

onboarding names requirements `satisfied_by: "identity.email_verified"`, which only works if
identity can be asked. It could not be, so those flows could never complete.

THREE OUTCOMES, and keeping them apart is the entire safety property:

  200 {"satisfied": true|false}  we know, and this is the answer
  404                            no such account — the caller reads this as UNSATISFIED, which
                                 is right: a person who does not exist has verified nothing
  501                            WE DO NOT ANSWER THAT QUESTION. The caller reads any non-404
                                 error as UNKNOWN, and unknown never counts as satisfied.

The third is why an unrecognised fact must not be a 404. A 404 would be read as a decision —
"this requirement is not met" — when the truth is that nobody evaluated it. For a requirement
that gates a welcome credit, the difference is whether a stranger is refused or quietly
onboarded.

post.description:
Erase a data subject. Called by compliance-service during a DSAR fan-out.

identity owns the pseudonym LINKAGE, so this is the call that actually makes the person
unlinkable everywhere else. Idempotent: a retry on an already-erased subject returns the same
shape rather than failing, because a DSAR retries.

post.description:
Clear ONE rate-limit key. The operator's 3am remedy.

Someone WILL be locked out by a misconfigured limit or a shared NAT. If the only tool is
FLUSHALL, the operator uses it and takes every other limit on the platform down with it. This
clears exactly one key and nothing else — the surgical alternative to the sledgehammer.

The key is the composite key the policy built (e.g. `auth|s:<subject>`); an operator reads it
off the throttled response's logs. It is internal-token gated: unblocking a limit is a platform
action, not a tenant one.

schema.title: X-Internal-Token
Response Ratelimit Unblock Internal Ratelimit Unblock Post

get.description:
The member directory for a background JOB — no user JWT required.

The user-facing read gates on a `members:read` CAPABILITY and takes the tenant off the caller's
token, which is exactly right for a person clicking a screen and wrong for a service. A document
renderer, an export worker, a billing sweep — these hold the INTERNAL token, not a user JWT with
caps, so they had no way to enumerate a tenant's members at all.

Here the tenant IS a parameter, and that is safe precisely because the caller is internal: it
holds the platform's service token and is trusted to name the tenant it is working for. It is
REQUIRED (min_length=1) — there is deliberately no "all tenants" value, so a bug that forgets to
set it fails loudly rather than dumping every company's staff. The projection is the same one the
admin route uses: identifier, roles, caps, status — never a credential.
